summary: A framework for how data plane protocols can be applied to operations and maintenance procedures for MPLS. It is organized around fault, configuration, accounting, performance, and security management, commonly called FCAPS. The document is informational.

eli5.summary: A map of the check-up tools for a label-based network, showing which tool helps with which kind of problem.

questions: how do you measure mpls network performance
subtitle: Framework for diagnosing and managing faults in label-switching networks.

tldr.problem: MPLS networks need to detect failures, diagnose problems, measure performance, and manage security, but there is no unified framework for how operations and management (OAM) tools should work together to address these needs.
tldr.mechanism: This framework shows how data plane OAM tools can be applied to the FCAPS model (Fault, Configuration, Accounting, Performance, Security management) for MPLS networks, outlining the types of failures to detect, how to diagnose them quickly, and what tools and techniques are needed.
tldr.outcome: The framework guides the design of MPLS OAM protocols and helps operators plan how to monitor and troubleshoot their label-switched networks.

today: RFC 4378 is an informational framework document that guides the design of MPLS OAM protocols. It remains a key reference for operators and protocol designers implementing fault detection, diagnosis, and performance monitoring in MPLS networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MPLS networks deliver data by forwarding packets based on labels (short identifiers) rather than full destination addresses. Like any network, they need operations and management (OAM) functions to stay healthy. OAM activities fall into five categories, commonly called FCAPS: Fault management (detecting and fixing problems), Configuration management (verifying settings), Accounting (tracking usage), Performance management (measuring speed and loss), and Security management (protecting the network).

This framework outlines how data plane OAM protocols (tools that work with actual packet flows rather than control systems) can address each FCAPS category for MPLS networks. The framework is structured around common failure scenarios, diagnostic techniques, and management tools.
sections.eli5: Labeled networks need a way to notice when something breaks, figure out what is wrong, measure how fast it is, and keep it safe. This document explains what kinds of tools help with each task.

sections.title: Fault Detection and Diagnosis
sections.content:
Fault detection means finding all data plane failures between a sender and receiver. Common failures include lower-layer faults (physical link problems), node failures (a router stops working), and MPLS mis-forwarding (where a router sends a packet to the wrong place because control plane and data plane are out of sync).

Mis-forwarding can take two forms: a packet arrives with a label that the next router does not recognize (No ILM condition), or a packet is forwarded to the wrong downstream label (wrong LSP). Other faults include MTU problems (packets too large to forward), TTL mishandling (hop-limit handling is inconsistent), congestion (too many packets), mis-ordering (packets arrive out of sequence), and payload corruption.

Diagnosis has two forms: characterization (finding the actual path a packet takes, including equal-cost multi-paths) and isolation (narrowing down where the fault occurred). Operators can detect faults locally and raise alarms, or detect them remotely and automatically restore service if possible. Response speed matters: SLAs require faults to be detected and resolved within a specific time budget.
sections.eli5: There are many things that can go wrong: broken links, broken routers, wrong routing decisions, packets that are too big, or too many packets at once. Finding the problem quickly is like following a trail from the symptom back to the cause.

sections.title: Configuration, Accounting, and Performance
sections.content:
Configuration management verifies that an LSP is set up correctly and that control plane information matches the data plane. An ad-hoc data plane probe can test path integrity and compare control plane configuration against what the probe discovers.

Accounting in MPLS does not have special OAM requirements beyond standard network accounting (measuring traffic volumes for billing).

Performance management measures the information transfer characteristics of LSPs, typically compared against a Service Level Agreement (SLA). Two key metrics are latency (and jitter, which is variation in latency) and loss. Latency can be measured with precisely synchronized clocks at sender and receiver (comparing timestamps in PDUs), or with ping-like probes that measure round-trip time (RTT) and infer one-way latency. Loss is measured by periodically reading ingress and egress counters from MIB modules, or by sending probe traffic that can also measure jitter and delay. Equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) load sharing means any single RTT measurement only represents one of several paths.
sections.eli5: Configuration checking makes sure the routing table matches the actual packets. Accounting counts the bytes. Performance checking measures how fast the network is and if any packets get lost.

sections.title: Security and OAM
sections.content:
OAM in a secure environment requires operators to filter OAM messages at network edges so malicious users cannot inject MPLS OAM transactions from outside the MPLS network. Provider-initiated OAM should not leak outside the MPLS cloud. Within a single provider domain, OAM is relatively straightforward, but in multi-provider deployments, authentication and authorization become critical: providers must verify that OAM traffic comes from authorized sources.

OAM tools themselves can address security concerns. Rigorous defect handling (detecting and reporting failures) offers customers integrity protection: operators can detect when VPN traffic leaks from one VPN into another. However, inter-provider OAM introduces risks: since portions of LSPs are outside a provider's control, attackers could inject traffic for denial-of-service attacks. OAM PDUs are not explicitly identified in the MPLS header, so transit routers do not typically inspect them. Tools that extract network information (like TTL-based probing) require authentication so unauthorized users cannot learn about network structure.
sections.eli5: Management tools must be locked down so only trusted people can use them. Well-designed tools can catch when data leaks from one customer to another, but tools can also leak information about how the network is built.

sections.title: Framework Summary
sections.content:
This framework organizes OAM needs for MPLS around the FCAPS model. Fault management requires tools to detect failures quickly (within the SLA time budget), diagnose their location, and measure service availability. Configuration management needs verification tools. Performance management requires latency and loss measurements. Security management requires filtering, authentication, and defect handling to protect both provider networks and customer VPNs.

Data plane OAM tools are the focus of this framework because they work with actual packet flows and can detect failures that control plane tools might miss. Examples include probe mechanisms (like ping), counter-based monitoring, and path discovery tools. The framework is technology-neutral: specific protocols such as MPLS ping or MPLS traceroute implement these functions, but the framework itself outlines the requirements they must meet.
sections.eli5: The framework ties different management tools together so operators know which tool finds which problem. Probing tools send test packets. Counting tools read statistics. Together they give a complete picture of network health.
